Defining
 
the
 
Boundaries
 
of
 
the
 
Knowledge
 
Domain
 
Before
 
analyzing
 
the
 
literature
 
in
 
detail,
 
it
 
is
 
important
 
to
 
acknowledge
 
that
 
the
 
research
 
problem
 
is
 
complex
 
and
 
multidisciplinary.
 
The
 
reviewed
 
studies
 
go
 
beyond
 
traditional
 
production
 

scheduling
 
and
 
encompass
 
optimization,
 
energy
 
management,
 
Digital
 
Twins,
 
Artificial
 
Intelligence,
 
Explainable
 
AI,
 
and
 
human-centered
 
manufacturing.
 
 
The
 
corpus
 
reveals
 
that
 
steel
 
manufacturing
 
can
 
no
 
longer
 
be
 
viewed
 
as
 
a
 
purely
 
operational
 
scheduling
 
problem.
 
Modern
 
production
 
systems
 
operate
 
in
 
dynamic
 
environments
 
characterized
 
by
 
uncertainty,
 
fluctuating
 
energy
 
demand,
 
real-time
 
decision
 
requirements,
 
and
 
increasing
 
sustainability
 
constraints.
 
As
 
a
 
result,
 
decision-making
 
must
 
integrate
 
data,
 
prediction,
 
optimization,
 
and
 
human
 
expertise.
 
To
 
address
 
this
 
complexity,
 
several
 
complementary
 
tools
 
are
 
employed
 
throughout
 
the
 
literature.
 
These
 
include
 
mathematical
 
optimization
 
methods
 
such
 
as
 
MILP,
 
robust
 
optimization,
 
and
 
multi-objective
 
optimization;
 
metaheuristic
 
approaches
 
such
 
as
 
Genetic
 
Algorithms,
 
NSGA-II,
 
and
 
Grey
 
Wolf
 
Optimization;
 
Digital
 
Twin
 
technologies
 
for
 
real-time
 
system
 
representation;
 
predictive
 
analytics
 
for
 
forecasting
 
industrial
 
events;
 
reinforcement
 
learning
 
techniques
 
for
 
adaptive
 
scheduling;
 
and
 
Explainable
 
AI
 
methods
 
to
 
improve
 
transparency
 
and
 
trust.
 
Based
 
on
 
the
 
analysis
 
of
 
the
 
corpus,
 
the
 
knowledge
 
domain
 
can
 
be
 
defined
 
as:
 
Intelligent,
 
energy-aware,
 
and
 
human-centered
 
scheduling
 
and
 
decision-making
 
in
 
steel
 
manufacturing
 
through
 
the
 
integration
 
of
 
optimization,
 
Digital
 
Twins,
 
Reinforcement
 
Learning,
 
Explainable
 
Artificial
 
Intelligence,
 
and
 
Industry
 
5.0
 
principles.
 
This
 
definition
 
captures
 
the
 
common
 
objective
 
shared
 
by
 
the
 
reviewed
 
studies:
 
developing
 
adaptive,
 
explainable,
 
and
 
efficient
 
production
 
systems
 
capable
 
of
 
supporting
 
industrial
 
decision-making
 
in
 
increasingly
 
complex
 
manufacturing
 
environments.

Task
 
3:
 
Synthesis
 
Divergence
 
The
 
topographical
 
mapping
 
revealed
 
that
 
the
 
literature
 
converges
 
toward
 
intelligent
 
and
 
adaptive
 
manufacturing
 
systems.
 
However,
 
the
 
corpus
 
also
 
contains
 
several
 
competing
 
approaches
 
that
 
create
 
strategic
 
tensions.
 
These
 
divergences
 
are
 
important
 
because
 
they
 
highlight
 
the
 
key
 
trade-offs
 
that
 
organizations
 
must
 
manage
 
when
 
designing
 
future
 
decision-support
 
systems
 
for
 
steel
 
manufacturing.
 
Optimization
 
vs
 
Reinforcement
 
Learning
 
A
 
first
 
divergence
 
concerns
 
the
 
choice
 
between
 
traditional
 
optimization
 
techniques
 
and
 
learning-based
 
approaches.
 
Classical
 
methods
 
such
 
as
 
MILP,
 
robust
 
optimization,
 
rolling-horizon
 
planning,
 
and
 
matheuristics
 
aim
 
to
 
generate
 
optimal
 
or
 
near-optimal
 
schedules
 
based
 
on
 
mathematical
 
models.
 
Their
 
main
 
strengths
 
are
 
transparency,
 
predictability,
 
and
 
ease
 
of
 
validation.
 
They
 
remain
 
particularly
 
valuable
 
in
 
environments
 
where
 
decision
 
reliability
 
is
 
critical.
 
In
 
contrast,
 
Reinforcement
 
Learning
 
approaches,
 
including
 
Deep
 
Reinforcement
 
Learning
 
(DRL),
 
Multi-Agent
 
Reinforcement
 
Learning
 
(MARL),
 
and
 
Deep
 
Q-Networks
 
(DQN),
 
learn
 
scheduling
 
policies
 
directly
 
from
 
operational
 
data
 
and
 
interactions
 
with
 
the
 
environment.
 
These
 
methods
 
are
 
better
 
suited
 
to
 
highly
 
dynamic
 
and
 
uncertain
 
production
 
contexts
 
but
 
are
 
often
 
more
 
difficult
 
to
 
interpret
 
and
 
validate.
 
Trade-off:
 
optimal
 
and
 
explainable
 
decisions
 
versus
 
adaptive
 
and
 
autonomous
 
decisions.
 
 
Static
 
Planning
 
Models
 
vs
 
Digital
 
Twins
 
A
 
second
 
divergence
 
appears
 
between
 
conventional
 
planning
 
systems
 
and
 
Digital
 
Twin-based
 
environments.
 
Traditional
 
scheduling
 
models
 
rely
 
primarily
 
on
 
predefined
 
parameters
 
and
 
historical
 
information.
 
They
 
are
 
relatively
 
simple
 
to
 
implement
 
but
 
frequently
 
struggle
 
to
 
react
 
quickly
 
to
 
operational
 
disturbances.
 

Digital
 
Twins
 
provide
 
a
 
continuously
 
synchronized
 
virtual
 
representation
 
of
 
the
 
physical
 
production
 
system.
 
By
 
integrating
 
real-time
 
data,
 
simulation
 
capabilities,
 
and
 
predictive
 
analytics,
 
they
 
support
 
dynamic
 
monitoring
 
and
 
real-time
 
decision-making.
 
Trade-off:
 
lower
 
implementation
 
costs
 
versus
 
greater
 
real-time
 
visibility,
 
flexibility,
 
and
 
responsiveness.
 
 
Reactive
 
vs
 
Predictive
 
Scheduling
 
The
 
literature
 
also
 
contrasts
 
different
 
approaches
 
to
 
uncertainty
 
management.
 
Reactive
 
scheduling
 
modifies
 
production
 
plans
 
after
 
disruptions
 
occur,
 
such
 
as
 
equipment
 
failures,
 
delays,
 
or
 
resource
 
shortages.
 
While
 
straightforward
 
to
 
implement,
 
it
 
often
 
results
 
in
 
operational
 
instability
 
and
 
increased
 
rescheduling
 
effort.
 
Predictive
 
scheduling
 
attempts
 
to
 
anticipate
 
disruptions
 
before
 
they
 
occur
 
through
 
forecasting
 
techniques,
 
predictive
 
analytics,
 
and
 
machine
 
learning
 
models.
 
These
 
approaches
 
improve
 
robustness
 
but
 
require
 
accurate
 
data
 
and
 
reliable
 
prediction
 
models.
 
Trade-off:
 
responding
 
to
 
disruptions
 
versus
 
anticipating
 
disruptions.
 
 
Black-Box
 
AI
 
vs
 
Explainable
 
AI
 
As
 
Artificial
 
Intelligence
 
becomes
 
increasingly
 
integrated
 
into
 
production
 
systems,
 
the
 
need
 
for
 
explainability
 
becomes
 
a
 
major
 
concern.
 
Advanced
 
AI
 
models
 
frequently
 
achieve
 
superior
 
prediction
 
and
 
optimization
 
performance
 
but
 
often
 
operate
 
as
 
black
 
boxes.
 
Their
 
decision-making
 
process
 
may
 
be
 
difficult
 
for
 
operators
 
and
 
managers
 
to
 
understand.
 
Explainable
 
AI
 
(XAI)
 
approaches
 
seek
 
to
 
overcome
 
this
 
limitation
 
through
 
transparency
 
assessment,
 
counterfactual
 
explanations,
 
and
 
interpretable
 
reinforcement
 
learning
 
methods.
 
These
 
mechanisms
 
improve
 
trust
 
and
 
facilitate
 
industrial
 
adoption.
 
Trade-off:
 
maximum
 
performance
 
versus
 
transparency
 
and
 
trust.
 
 

Automation
 
vs
 
Human-Centric
 
Industry
 
5.0
 
The
 
final
 
divergence
 
concerns
 
the
 
role
 
of
 
humans
 
in
 
future
 
manufacturing
 
systems.
 
Some
 
studies
